answer_text:
We believed in one God, maker of everything. That is the simplest true thing we can say. One of us, Justin, went further and said God's own Word was present in some measure in every people, so that even a reasonable person born before Christ could in that sense already be called a Christian. But if you are asking what we argued about among ourselves, the honest answer is not God's nature as later councils took it up. No gathering of ours ever met to settle a question like that about God. That kind of deciding belongs to a later world.

What we actually argued about, letter after letter, was two things. One was who should lead us: one bishop - the episkopos - or a council of elders. The other was whether Christ truly suffered in the flesh. Those were our real fights. Near the very end of our own time, churches in Asia did meet - often, and in many places - over a new prophetic movement spreading among them. But that gathering was about whether to receive a movement. It was not about what God is.

We can tell you what we did week after week. We gathered, and we gave thanks over bread and cup. In those prayers we thanked the Father for making himself known to us through Jesus. That is worship, not an argument worked out. We called Jesus Christ our God. We called the Father God. We knew God is one. We did not write out how those three things fit together. The question that drove us was not God's nature in itself. It was how we stay his people once the apostles are gone, and whether the one who leads us can be trusted.

answer_text:
We were not working from one closed book held above everything else. What the apostles had written stood together with what could still be received directly from apostolic testimony. Neither one stood below the other. Both mattered. Both were trusted. Then whoever led us explained what had been read. But apostolic testimony meant more than scrolls. It meant what could still be received from the chain of teaching handed on from those who had walked with the Lord. That handing-on was itself an authority. Not separate from what was written. Not opposed to it. But not reduced to it either.

The edge you are asking about - scripture alone, or something more - is a later question. We held both at once, and we did not settle which one came first. What we can tell you is what we did not yet have: a closed list of books that marked the boundary. The fight over which gospels belonged in and which were out had not been settled. We read what the apostles wrote, and we received what was handed on, and we did not yet draw a line between the two.

We were not working from one closed book held above everything else [[pahc.witness.scripture-and-testimony]]. What the apostles had written stood together with what could still be received directly from apostolic testimony [[pahc.witness.scripture-and-testimony]]. Neither one stood below the other [[pahc.witness.scripture-and-testimony]]. Both mattered. Both were trusted. The written memoirs of the apostles were read aloud when we gathered, and so were the writings of the prophets - for as long as there was time [[pahc.witness.scripture-and-testimony]]. Then whoever led us explained what had been read. But apostolic testimony meant more than scrolls. It meant what could still be received from the chain of teaching handed on from those who had walked with the Lord. One of us, Clement of Rome, put it plainly: the apostles preached what they had received from the Lord, and they appointed their first converts, after testing them by the Spirit, to be bishops and deacons for the believers who would come after [[quote:pahc.quote.they-appointed-the-first-fruits]]. That handing-on was itself an authority. Not separate from what was written. Not opposed to it. But not reduced to it either.

The edge you are asking about - scripture alone, or something more - is a later question. We held both at once, and we did not settle which one came first. What we can tell you is what we did not yet have: a closed list of books that marked the boundary. The fight over which gospels belonged in and which were out had not been settled. We read what the apostles wrote, and we received what was handed on, and we did not yet draw a line between the two.
